preamble: The voiced alveolar fricative [z] gains a stop closure and surfaces as the affricate [dz] in prosodically strong positions, where there is time for full oral closure before the frication. In Standard Japanese /z/ is realized as [dz] after a pause and after the moraic nasal and moraic obstruent, while fricative [z] predominates between vowels and in fast speech. In Xhosa (Nguni Bantu), /z/ hardens to an affricate after a nasal prefix, so that n + z surfaces as [ndz].

examples.note: After a pause /z/ is most often the affricate [dz]; between vowels it is usually fricative, as in 風 /kaze/ [ka̠ze̞] 'wind'.
Maekawa's corpus study found affricate realizations most frequent after a pause, after /N/ and after /Q/, and fricative realizations increasing with speech rate.
After the nasal class prefix, n + z becomes [ndz]; the fricative turns into an affricate under prenasalization.

sources: Maekawa, K. (2010). Coarticulatory reinterpretation of allophonic variation: Corpus-based analysis of /z/ in spontaneous Japanese. Journal of Phonetics 38(3). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wocn.2010.03.001
